Guttural describes a sound — usually a voice, a word, or a language — that is harsh, rough, and seems to come from deep in the throat, almost like a growl or a rasp. If a sound feels like it is being scraped or rumbled out from the back of the throat rather than formed smoothly at the lips or tip of the tongue, it is guttural.
What Does It Actually Sound Like?

Think about these sounds and compare them:

  • The soft sound of someone whispering "hello" → Not guttural.
  • A man clearing his throat loudly → Guttural.
  • A light, airy laugh → Not guttural.
  • A low, gravelly growl from a guard dog → Guttural.
  • The smooth sound of "la la la" → Not guttural.
  • The harsh, scratchy sound of gargling water → Guttural.

The common thread is this: guttural sounds feel deep, raw, rough, and throat-driven. They have texture and weight. They are not clean or delicate. They come from the back of the throat and often carry a slightly animal or primal quality.
The Two Main Ways It Is Used

1. In Everyday Language (the most common use)

This is how most people use the word. It describes any voice or sound that strikes you as rough, low, and throaty — almost like a growl.

  • A man recovering from laryngitis might speak in a guttural voice.
  • A villain in a movie might deliver his lines in a guttural whisper.
  • An injured animal might let out a guttural cry.
  • Thunder rolling close by might be described as a guttural rumble.

Here, the word is not being used scientifically. It is describing the quality and feel of a sound — one that is raw, rough, and deep.

2. In Language and Linguistics (the technical use)

In the study of language, guttural describes specific speech sounds that are physically produced at the back of the throat. These are consonants made not with the lips or the front of the tongue, but deep in the mouth — near the throat.

For example:

  • The "kh" sound in Arabic (like in the name "Khalid") is a guttural sound — produced far back in the throat with a friction-like rasp.
  • The French "r" sound, which many English speakers find difficult, is also considered guttural because it is made at the back of the throat with a slight vibration.
  • The "ch" sound in the Scottish word "loch" is another example — it is not a clean sound like "k"; it has a harsh, throaty quality.

This is why certain languages — like Arabic, German, Hebrew, and Dutch — are sometimes described as guttural languages. They contain a relatively high number of sounds that are produced deep in the throat and that carry that characteristic harshness.
The Feeling and Connotation of the Word

Beyond the physical description, the word guttural carries a certain mood. When a writer calls something guttural, they are usually suggesting something that feels:

  • Primal — like an instinctive, unpolished sound from deep inside a person or animal.
  • Intense — guttural sounds rarely feel soft or gentle; they feel forceful and raw.
  • Slightly rough or unrefined — not always in a negative way, but in the sense that it is not smooth or pretty.

For example: "He let out a guttural scream" tells you far more than just "he screamed." It tells you the scream was raw, ragged, and came from somewhere deep — almost animal. It creates a very specific image.

It is worth being clear about what the word does not mean:

  • It does not mean loud. A voice can be guttural and quiet at the same time (a low, raspy whisper, for instance).
  • It does not mean rude or offensive (that would be "crude" or "vulgar"). Guttural is purely about sound quality.
  • It does not mean slow or heavy. A fast sound can still be guttural if it is rough and throat-driven.

Guttural = a sound that is harsh, raw, rough, and produced deep in the throat — whether you are describing a person's gravelly voice, an animal's growl, a foreign language sound, or any sound that feels like it is being dragged up from the base of the throat rather than shaped smoothly at the front of the mouth.

The next time you hear someone speak in a very deep, scratchy, raspy voice — or hear a language with a lot of harsh throat sounds — the word you are looking for is guttural.
